cases.name: dev-crop-type-sentinel2
cases.promptMarkdown:
I'm doing a master's project on crop type classification from Sentinel-2 image time series. I need ground-truth labels for actual crops (wheat, maize, rapeseed and so on, not just cropland versus non-cropland) for individual fields or pixels, already paired with multi-temporal Sentinel-2 data, because I don't have time to build my own download and preprocessing pipeline. The data also needs a licence that lets me publish results and share trained models. Which benchmark datasets fit, and where do I get them?

Please search the web rather than answering from memory, and check that each dataset you recommend really exists and how it can be accessed.

graders.name: 01-recall-breizhcrops
graders.evidence:
Five datasets fit. All have real crop-type labels (not just cropland versus non-cropland) paired with Sentinel-2 time series, and all have licences that allow publishing results and sharing models. I confirmed each one exists. I could only confirm some of the licence and access details directly. The rest come from search summaries, and I've marked which.

## Recommended

**1. EuroCropsML (parcel-level time series, the easiest to start with)**
- It has 706,683 parcels in 176 crop classes, from Latvia, Portugal and Estonia in 2021. Each parcel is a time series of median Sentinel-2 L1C reflectance, with labels from farmer declarations (EuroCrops v9).
- Get it from Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10629609; versions such as [10683255](https://zenodo.org/records/10683255)), or with `pip install eurocropsml` followed by `eurocropsml-cli datasets eurocrops download`.
- Licence: the paper is CC BY 4.0 and the code is MIT. I did not read the licence on the Zenodo record itself, so check it before you publish. EuroCrops is built from national sources with differing terms.
- It is built for few-shot and transfer experiments (pretrain on Latvia and Portugal, fine-tune on Estonia). It also works as a plain classification benchmark.
- A "2.0" version with more countries is mentioned in a recent paper. I did not verify it.

**2. PASTIS / PASTIS-R (parcel segmentation of France)**
- It has 2,433 patches of 128×128 pixels at 10 m, with 18 crop types plus background and void. The labels are per parcel, and the patches are Sentinel-2 time series. PASTIS-R adds Sentinel-1.
- I confirmed that the [PASTIS Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/5012942) exists. It is a single 28.8 GB file, licensed CC BY 4.0.
- PASTIS-R is at zenodo.org/record/5735646. I only saw that link on a secondary summary page, so open it to confirm. There is also a [Hugging Face TACO copy](https://huggingface.co/datasets/isp-uv-es/pastis-r-taco) under CC-BY-4.0.
- The Zenodo page doesn't describe the labels or mention Sentinel-2 itself. That comes from the paper and the secondary sources.

**3. BreizhCrops (Brittany, France, 2017)**
- It has about 610k–768k field-level time series, depending on the processing level, with top- and bottom-of-atmosphere versions. Labels come from the French RPG. The class count is reported as nine in one source. I couldn't confirm that.
- Install with `pip install breizhcrops`, then `breizhcrops.BreizhCrops("frh04")`. The data is also on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/14585341).
- Licence: the Zenodo record and arXiv listing say CC BY 4.0. The code repository ([dl4sits/BreizhCrops](https://github.com/dl4sits/BreizhCrops)) is GPL-3.0, which applies to the code, not the data. The paper only says the RPG labels are under an "open license".
- It is small and simple, so it works well for quick baselines.

**4. AgriSen-COG (Austria, Belgium, Catalonia, Denmark and the Netherlands, 2019–2020)**
- The labels are parcel-level from the LPIS (the EU's parcel registry). The data is Sentinel-2 in cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs, built for segmentation and classification.
- The [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/7892012) is CC BY 4.0. Its files (parcel info, original LPIS, ground-truth patches) were listed. I did not check whether the Sentinel-2 imagery is on Zenodo or comes from the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/tselea/agrisen-cog), so read the repo's instructions.
- The paper says the LPIS data is under the Open Data Commons Attribution Licence, which allows publishing.

**5. Sen4AgriNet (Catalonia and France, 2016–2020)**
- It has about 225,000 multi-year patches (about 10 TB), with a parcel-aggregated version and a patch version. Labels are from the LPIS.
- The Hugging Face copy is [isp-uv-es/sen4agrinet-taco](https://huggingface.co/datasets/isp-uv-es/sen4agrinet-taco). The experiment code is in [Orion-AI-Lab/S4A-Models](https://github.com/Orion-AI-Lab/S4A-Models) (MIT).
- The licence is inconsistent. The journal version says CC BY 4.0, while arXiv and Hugging Face say CC BY-SA 4.0. Under share-alike, anything you share that is derived from the data may have to carry the same licence. That could matter for sharing models, so ask your supervisor or check the official release.
- At 10 TB it is probably too big for a master's project unless you use a subset.

## Not recommended for your case
- **CropHarvest:** it is global but mostly binary crop versus non-crop labels, so it doesn't meet your requirement.
- **EuroCrops:** it is labels only, with no Sentinel-2 data. Use EuroCropsML instead.
- **ZueriCrop and TimeMatch:** I did not verify their licences or access, so I'm not recommending them.

## Suggested path
Start with **BreizhCrops** or **EuroCropsML** for a quick time-series classification baseline. Use **PASTIS-R** if you want image-level or segmentation models. Add **AgriSen-COG** if you need more countries.

Some pages were blocked or incomplete (Nature, PMC, ResearchGate, and the arXiv PDF text). So the EuroCropsML and Sen4AgriNet details rest on search summaries. Before you publish, read each Zenodo or Hugging Face licence field, and cite the original papers.

Sources:
- [EuroCropsML (Nature Sci. Data)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-04952-7)
- [EuroCropsML (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12009327/)
- [EuroCropsML on GitHub](https://github.com/dida-do/eurocropsml)
- [eurocropsml on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/eurocropsml/)
- [PASTIS on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/5012942)
- [PASTIS-R summary](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/pastis-r-benchmark)
- [BreizhCrops on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.11893)
- [BreizhCrops on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/14585341)
- [AgriSen-COG paper](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15122980)
- [Sen4AgriNet paper (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.00951v2)
- [EuroCrops (Nature Sci. Data)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02517-0)

graders.evidence:
Four datasets fit your criteria. Two are plain downloads, one needs a short application, and one is mostly out of reach for a benchmark. I confirmed the London and Zenodo download details by opening those pages. The ISSDA and Pecan Street access details come from search results only, because the ISSDA page returned a 403 when I tried to open it.

## Download directly (no application)

**1. Low Carbon London (UK Power Networks)**
- **What it covers:** 5,567 London households, half-hourly kWh, November 2011 to February 2014. About 1,100 were on dynamic time-of-use tariffs during 2013, and the rest were on a flat tariff. Each row has a household ID, a timestamp and the ACORN group.
- **Access:** Direct links with no login mentioned. The licence is CC BY 4.0. The full file is a 765 MB ZIP holding one CSV of about 167M rows. There is also a split version (168 CSVs) and a 2013 tariffs spreadsheet.
- **Source:** [London Datastore](https://data.london.gov.uk/dataset/smartmeter-energy-use-data-in-london-households/)
- **Copies:**
  - [Kaggle "Smart meters in London"](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/jeanmidev/smart-meters-in-london) adds weather and bank holidays. It needs a Kaggle account.
  - [Zenodo, forecasting-ready, 5,560 series](https://zenodo.org/records/4656091) is open and CC BY 4.0. The version I opened is the one without missing values.
  - [Zenodo, version with missing values](https://zenodo.org/records/4656072)
- **Caveats:**
  - Many households have only a partial history. Not every home has a full year, so check coverage per household.
  - The Zenodo "without missing values" version forward-fills gaps. Consider whether that suits a benchmark.

**2. GoiEner (Spain)**
- **What it covers:** 25,559 hourly series, November 2014 to June 2022, averaging nearly three years each. Raw and imputed versions are provided, plus metadata.
- **Access:** Open on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0. The raw files are 2.0 GB compressed and 15.1 GB uncompressed.
- **Source:** [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/7362094), described in [Scientific Data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02846-0).
- **Caveat:** The customers include shops, offices and industrial sites as well as homes. Filter them out using the metadata file before benchmarking on households only.

## Application required

**3. Irish CER Smart Metering Trial (ISSDA)**
- **What it covers:** About 4,200 households, half-hourly, July 2009 to December 2010, which is about 18 months. It also has household surveys and the time-of-use tariff trial design.
- **Access:** Search results say it is now on ISSDA Dataverse (DOI 10.7929/ISSDA/BX59EU). You request access and email a signed data request form to issda@ucd.ie. Once approved, you download it directly.
- **Conditions:** Research or teaching use only, for the named project, with all team members listed. The form must be signed for your organisation, and commercial use isn't allowed.
- **Sources:** [ISSDA access page](https://www.ucd.ie/issda/accessdata/) and [ISSDA FAQs](https://www.ucd.ie/issda/faqs/). I couldn't open the dataset page itself, so check the current terms there.

## Probably not suitable

- **Pecan Street Dataport:** It has 15-minute or finer data, but this is a US dataset and the free university tier is small. Search results say 75 homes, though a 2025 post suggests a larger sample, and the sources don't agree. You need an account approved with proof of university affiliation. Full access costs thousands of dollars. See [licences](https://www.pecanstreet.org/dataport/licenses/).
- **SERL Observatory (UK):** It has half-hourly data, but only through a secure researcher-access setup, so it isn't an open download.
- **Ausgrid Solar Home:** It has 300 homes with half-hourly data and rooftop solar. That is below your "hundreds" threshold and the homes are a solar-only population. See the [Ausgrid page](https://www.ausgrid.com.au/Industry/Our-Research/Data-to-share/Solar-home-electricity-data). I didn't check its current access terms.

## Recommendation

Start with Low Carbon London, filtered to households with at least a year of continuous data. GoiEner is the best second dataset because it is much larger, covers a different country, and some homes have several years of history. If you can wait on paperwork, add the Irish CER trial for a third climate and tariff context. Using several datasets also shows whether your benchmark results generalize.

- [ISSDA FAQs](https://www.ucd.ie/issda/faqs/)

- [Ausgrid solar home data](https://www.ausgrid.com.au/Industry/Our-Research/Data-to-share/Solar-home-electricity-data)

graders.name: 01-recall-physionet-2019-sepsis-challenge
graders.evidence:
For a baseline in a week, start with the PhysioNet 2019 Challenge data today. At the same time, begin the PhysioNet credentialing for MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD, because that process is the bottleneck. I confirmed every dataset below exists and how it is accessed by reading its source page or searching for it. Some details come only from search summaries, and I've flagged those.

## Download today, no application

**PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2019, "Early Prediction of Sepsis from Clinical Data" (v1.0.0)**
- It is open access under CC BY 4.0. Download it with `wget -r -N -c -np https://physionet.org/files/challenge-2019/1.0.0/`.
- It has 40,336 ICU stays in two training sets (A: 20,336 and B: 20,000). It is 42 MB, with one pipe-separated file per patient. Columns are hourly vitals, labs, demographics, and `SepsisLabel`.
- The label is time-stamped. For sepsis patients, `SepsisLabel` is 1 from 6 hours before the Sepsis-3-derived onset time. For other patients it is always 0.
- The label is already offset by 6 hours, and the data are hourly and pre-aggregated. This is fine for a baseline, but it limits what you can do about label definitions or finer time resolution.
- The hidden test set is not public, so you will have to create your own splits.

The open demo subsets of MIMIC and eICU are also available now, but they are too small for anything beyond testing your pipeline.

## Credentialed, same PhysioNet application

Both datasets below use one PhysioNet credentialing, so you apply once.

1. Register a PhysioNet account.
2. Complete the CITI course "Data or Specimens Only Research" and upload the completion report.
3. Submit your affiliation and reference details, and wait for approval.
4. Sign the dataset-specific DUA (PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data Use Agreement 1.5.0). Each dataset needs its own signature.

One secondary source reported approval taking about 1–2 weeks, which I did not confirm on a PhysioNet page. Plan for it to miss your one-week deadline, so submit it today. Your supervisor may need to act as your reference, and your institution may need to confirm your affiliation.

## Suggestions for deep learning
- **Sample size:** All of these are small, at about 30 to 110 speakers each. Split train and test **by speaker**, not by file, or your accuracy will be inflated. Leave-one-dataset-out testing is better still.
- **Where to start:** MDVR-KCL and the Italian set are the easiest to get today. Request NeuroVoz and PC-GITA early, since approval can take days or weeks.
- **Pooling:** Combining datasets gives you more data. But the language, microphone and task differ between them, and the model can learn to identify the dataset instead of the disease. Check for that.
- **Versions:** The NeuroVoz versions differ. The paper and Zenodo record say 112 speakers, while the GitHub README says 108 speakers and 2,903 files. Use the latest Zenodo record and cite the Scientific Data paper (Mendes-Laureano et al., 2024).
